title: The Geologist Who Fed a Billion People
event_summary: In August 1960, Mexican soil scientist Evangelina Villegas began her decades-long research at the International Maize and Wheat Improvement Center (CIMMYT) near Chapingo, ultimately developing Quality Protein Maize (QPM) — a biofortified corn variety with double the essential amino acids of normal maize. Working in near-obscurity alongside fellow scientist Surinder Vasal, she solved a problem that had stumped plant breeders for a century: how to make the opaque-2 gene, which boosted lysine and tryptophan content, compatible with high-yield farming. By the 1990s, QPM was being planted across 25 countries, rescuing millions of malnourished children in sub-Saharan Africa and Central America from kwashiorkor and stunted growth.
why_forgotten: The Green Revolution narrative was dominated by Norman Borlaug and his wheat varieties, while Villegas's quieter, longer work on maize protein went largely uncelebrated. As a Mexican woman scientist working in a male-dominated field during the Cold War era, her contributions were routinely credited to institutions rather than to her personally. She received the World Food Prize only in 2000, four decades after she began, and even then received minimal global press coverage.
why_it_matters: Today, QPM varieties feed hundreds of millions of people across Africa, Asia, and Latin America, and remain the primary tool for combating protein deficiency in maize-dependent populations. Her work proved that biofortification — breeding nutrition directly into staple crops — was viable at scale, laying the intellectual groundwork for Golden Rice and iron-fortified beans. Without Villegas's breakthrough, the modern biofortification movement that the WHO and Gates Foundation now champion would likely not exist.
